en: The Philippine tarsier has enormous eyes that are actually larger than its brain to help it hunt insects in the dark.
The giant Rafflesia found in Mindanao is a parasitic plant that lacks leaves, stems, and roots, relying entirely on its host vine.
Tamaraws, which are small water buffaloes endemic to Mindoro, have V-shaped horns and primarily eat grass in tropical mountain forests.
The Aedes aegypti mosquito, which transmits dengue fever in the Philippines, lays its eggs in clean, stagnant water found in tires and bottles.
The International Rice Research Institute in Laguna develops new rice varieties to help Filipino farmers grow more food and resist pests.
Whale sharks, locally called butanding, visit Donsol, Sorsogon to feed on tiny plankton, using their wide mouths to filter water.
Eating calamansi, a local citrus fruit rich in vitamin C, helps the human body absorb iron from plant-based foods like malunggay.
Mangrove trees in Panguil Bay have specialized stilt roots that anchor them in soft mud and filter salt from ocean water.
The Philippine eagle, one of the world's largest and most powerful eagles, hunts monkeys and flying lemurs in Mindanao forest canopies.
The pitcher plant of Mount Hamiguitan catches and digests insects in its modified leaves to survive in nutrient-poor mountain soil.
The Philippine crocodile, a critically endangered reptile, lives in freshwater marshes and lakes, where it builds nests from vegetation and mud.
Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park in the Sulu Sea contains hundreds of coral species that provide shelter for thousands of marine fish.
